cells.tense: You're bringing this through to the end right now, and you're the one holding it.
cells.verb: tending what grows, two demands kept in balance by care rather than force
cells.place: at the point where a thing is finished and ready to leave your hands
cells.ask: tell one person what this cost you to carry — plainly, once — and then let the finished thing go, not because you lost it but because it's done
cells.core: You're bringing this through to the end right now, and you're the one holding it. There are two things pulling on you and you haven't dropped either — you've kept them both fed, steadily, without squeezing. The thing is nearly whole, and you can feel that it's ready to leave your hands. Finishing it doesn't close anything; it opens the next one. What's open to you now is letting someone see what the carrying cost. Not for credit — so the letting go is witnessed, and lands as completion rather than loss.
cells.sheetLine: You've tended this to the finish and you can let it go whole.

cells.tense: You're bracing for what happens to this after you stop tending it.
cells.verb: tending what already grew, past the point where it needed you
cells.place: at a finish line you keep walking back across to check on
cells.ask: spend one hour taking in what's actually done — tasting it, enjoying it — instead of maintaining it, and let the satisfaction arrive before you reach for the next fix
cells.core: You're bracing for what happens to this after you stop tending it. It's finished — or close enough that the remaining work is yours to invent — and you keep finding one more thing to adjust, one more risk to cover, somewhere ahead where it falls apart without you. The care that grew this is now the thing keeping it from being done. Holding on this hard costs you the ease that care was supposed to make. The way back isn't less care; it's letting what's finished actually fill you — sitting with what you made long enough to feel that it's real, and that it's enough.
cells.sheetLine: It's done. You're still tending it.

cells.tense: You stopped tending this before it was finished, and you're still standing where you stopped.
cells.verb: the care that keeps something growing until it's whole
cells.place: at a door into the next thing that's already behind you
cells.ask: say out loud, to yourself or to someone, what this was for in the first place — the hope, not the task — and let that pull you back toward it rather than pushing yourself to the chore
cells.core: You stopped tending this before it was finished, and you're still standing where you stopped. The pieces are there, half-grown; the two things you were balancing both got set down. It isn't that you don't know how to finish — the finishing just lost its reason somewhere back there, and without a reason the care dried up. Pushing yourself at the unfinished work won't refill it. What refills it is the wanting underneath: remembering what you were growing this toward, and letting that hope do the pulling. When the hope is alive again, the tending comes back on its own, and it stops feeling like force.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down short of done and haven't moved from the spot.

cells.tense: You're already the one bringing this through, and you're calling it things working out.
cells.verb: tending two demands at once so that both come to completion
cells.place: right at the finish, where the thing leaves your hands whole
cells.ask: name one finished thing as something you carried — say what it took, once, to one person — and then let it go as yours, not as luck
cells.core: You're already the one bringing this through, and you're calling it things working out. Somebody kept both sides fed, made the quiet trade-offs, brought it to the end without dropping either — and that was you, every day, mostly without noticing. The tending is running; the ownership isn't. What's missing is simple and earlier than it sounds: saying that it cost you something, out loud, where someone can hear it. Once the carrying is claimed, the letting go stops looking like things slipping away and starts feeling like what it is — finished, and set down on purpose.
cells.sheetLine: You tended this to the finish. You're still calling it luck.
